questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Personally, I wanted to experience the Southern European way of life, especially of the Iberean peninsula.
Also, experiencing how different universities across Europe compares to that of KU.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
Whilst Lisbon is an amazing city and Portugal is a lovely country with so many things to see and do, the university does leave a lot to be desired. Housing quality is not that good, and if you live in Lisbon, the time spent on getting to the university can be quite high.

A more personal complaint is, that both the university and Lisbon itself are very dominated by tourism, digital nomads and other international students. So you will probably not get the authentic Portuguese experience and you are quite unlikely to make any Portuguese friends. In Lisbon you are just another foreigner.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Whilst you do get sent some information by the administration, you do have to find a lot of the information yourself. Some information can be a bit difficult to find, and I found myself often being unsure if I had found the right place.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Very easy. There are plenty of website offering housing for students in Lisbon.
I used Uniplaces, which got the job done - though they do charge a hefty commission of 200 EUR.
It is in general a good idea to look for housing as early as possible, and through as many websites as possible.
A friend of mine booked almost a year in advance and got a much better value-for-money than anyone else.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
Most exchange students choose to live in Lisbon proper, and in general there is not much to do near campus except for going surfing and/or going to the beach.
Though, those exchange students who lived on campus semmed to have a decent community together.

Getting to campus takes 40-50 minutes each way from Cais do Sodré station, and trains only run every 20 minutes outside of rush-hour. So you will spend a lot of time on commuting. I would recommend living near Cais do Sodré/Santos/Alcantara station or close to the green metro line.

During my stay the train drivers were near constantly on strike (Spring 2023), and the train company did not provide bus-replacements to compensate. That meant that often there were only 1 train per hour, which was always completely full.

Another thing to consider, is that the railway line will soon (2024/2025) undergo major renovations. In case of track-works the train company should be providing replacement-busses, but it is still something to consider.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: In general, you won't find housing for under 450 EUR a month in Lisbon, and the quality of housing is in general also quite low.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
It can be quite hard to find the correct list of courses (compared to KU), likewise course descriptions for some courses can be very unfulfilling.
The first point caused me a lot of trouble for the OLA, which severely delayed the payment of the Erasmus Grant.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
For master students there is a bidding system, where you are allocated a number of points that you can spend on the courses that you want. The courses are then allocated to those who have spent the largest number of point on a given course.

Courses that you may want, can have overlapping schedules either for classes or the examns. 
This makes planning for what courses to bid on very tedious and it is quite likely that you have to make compromises, to make them fit into the schedule.

Another point of bother was that the bidding only started two weeks ahead of the beginninig of classes, which again was a cause of uncertainty.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
Very limited.
During a presentation by some of the staff, one of them mentioned, that exchange students tend to find the system confusing and/or annoying, but that they nevertheless insisted it is a good system.
Likewise, local students also think the system is stupid.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the courses that I planned on getting, and it is usually not a problem that people get denied for their courses after the bidding.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Don't think too hard about it!
Most courses are not of that high a level, so it is not like you are going to be missing out on that much either way.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
Most courses were of level that were a step or two beneath that of KU.
In general there were few courses specific to Economics.
The courses you can choose are either for 3,5 ECTS or 7 ECTS. Those of 3 ECTS can have a quite limited scope in terms of content

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
In most courses you only have lectures by the professor and only 3 hours a week.
The final grade usually only consists of 50% from the exam. Where the rest can be divided into class participation, class presentations, quizzes in class and assignments.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
-Political Economy
-Macroeconomics of Financial Markets
-Data Analytics for Finance
-Banking
-Introduction to Programming

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
-I thought Political Economy gave a good introduction to what political economics is about. Though, you do not go that deep into each theory as you would at KU, you do get introduced to a lot of different fields, where you can apply an economics mindset to political theories and dilemmas.

-Macroeconomics of Financial Markets shares some elements with Macro III, but focuses a on financial markets instead. The difficulty is not that high though.

-Introduction to Programming gives you a bit of insight into how Python works in regards to flow control, classes and functions. If you've already had Introduction to Social Data Science at KU it should be quite easy for you.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: In general most things are a lot cheaper than in Copenhagen, with the exception of some things in grocery stores, which can be compareble to those in Copenhagen.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: NOVA SBE does have some cultural, athletic and social activities. I didn't really engange in any of them.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: There are plenty of things to do in Lisbon, so just do what you like doing, whether it is linked to the university or not.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
There are so many things to do in and around Portugal.
In Portugal outside of the Lisbon area there is: Porto, Coimbra, the Algarve Coast to name a few.
There are the Azores islands - especially São Miguel and Terceira Island, and also Madeira.
Spain is next door with amazing cities like Santiagio de Compostela, Madrid, Cadiz, Sevilla, Cordoba, Granada, Malaga, Bilbao, San Sebastian, Valencia.
Morocco is also very close.
So look for cheap plane tickets on Ryanair, Vueling, Easyjet, Azores Airlines.
And for bus tickets there is Flixbus and
ALSA.es
If you like football you can very easily become a member of SL Benfica, which cost 12 EUR a month and gives you a discount for match tickets and gives you priority for buying tickets.
There is also Sporting CP which is another big club in Lisbon.
Likewise, there is a football club in Estoril close to campus who also play in the best league in Portugal.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, NOVA SBE and Lisbon is a very international place.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: This does not really happen unless you know someone in advance, even though Portuguese people are extremely friendly and are very good at speaking English

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
Quality of life.
Food is great and cheap - as is wine and beer
Very nice weather.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
-Enjoy the country, enjoy the sun, enjoy the food and the wine and beer.
-The more time you spend outside and with friends the better.
-Don't think too hard about your studies.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think I got pretty much everything covered.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Enjoying life.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer:
Coping with all the tourists that floods the street of Lisbon and all the scammers that comes along with them.

And the low quality of housing

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
